title.raw: Head Injuries: Types, Severity, Red Flags, and When to Call 911
title.rendered: Head Injuries: Types, Severity, Red Flags, and When to Call 911

content.raw:
Head injuries range from a minor bump that resolves in an hour to a brain bleed that demands surgery within minutes. Most home falls and sports knocks fall in the mild end of that spectrum. A small but important fraction don't, and the trick is knowing which is which before the situation escalates.

This guide walks through the types of head injuries, the symptoms by severity, and when an injury becomes a 911 call. It also covers why kids follow different rules than adults. For the broader red-flag list across all medical emergencies, see our medical emergency signs guide.

If you already know you need ER care, see our head injury treatment page. It covers what we offer at ER of Lufkin and how to get seen fast.

What Counts as a Head Injury? Mild to Severe

A head injury is any trauma to the scalp, skull, or brain caused by an external force. The force can be a direct blow (a fall onto the floor), an accelerative jolt (whiplash from a car accident), or a penetrating object. Severity grades range from mild concussion to severe traumatic brain injury (TBI).

The everyday version most people see is mild. A bump on the head, brief dizziness, a headache for a few hours, then back to normal within a day or two. Per MedlinePlus, most head injuries are mild and recover fully with rest.

The severe end is rarer but unmistakable. Loss of consciousness, severe persistent headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, fluid leaking from the nose or ears, or a seizure all qualify. These need a 911 call, not a wait-and-see approach.

The middle ground is where the decision-making matters most. The next sections cover how to recognize where on the spectrum you are.

Types of Head Injuries: Concussion, Contusion, Hematoma, Skull Fracture

The head-injury differential includes several distinct injury patterns. Each has a different mechanism, prognosis, and treatment.

Concussion is the most common type. It is a temporary disruption of brain function from a jolt or blow, usually without bleeding or structural injury on imaging.

Symptoms include brief confusion, headache, dizziness, and sometimes a few seconds of disorientation. See our concussion treatment page for the full care path.

Contusion is a bruise on the brain itself. It happens when the brain strikes the inside of the skull during a sharp deceleration. Per NIH NINDS, contusions are usually mild but can swell over hours and need monitoring.

Subdural and epidural hematomas are blood collections between the skull and the brain. Subdurals build slowly over hours to days; epidurals build fast within minutes from a torn artery and are surgical emergencies.

Skull fracture is a break in the skull bone. Linear fractures often heal without surgery; depressed or basilar fractures (with fluid leaking from nose or ears) need surgical evaluation.

Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is widespread microscopic damage to nerve fibers from rotational forces. It is the type of injury most associated with high-speed crashes and prolonged unconsciousness.

Per the CDC TBI overview, even patients who appear fine after a head injury can develop bleeding hours later. Watchful 24-hour monitoring is the default for any moderate or severe injury.

Symptoms by Severity: Mild, Moderate, Severe

Head injury symptoms group into three severity bands. The pattern matters because the right next step depends on which band the injury falls into.

Mild head injury typically presents with brief headache, mild dizziness, a small bump or scalp laceration, and full clarity within minutes. No vomiting, no loss of consciousness, no confusion lasting more than a minute.

Mild injuries usually resolve within 24 to 48 hours with rest, fluids, and avoidance of screens or strenuous activity. If symptoms worsen, the picture shifts to moderate.

Moderate head injury presents with persistent headache, mild persistent confusion, light sensitivity, brief loss of consciousness (under a minute), or a single episode of vomiting. These symptoms warrant a same-day doctor visit or ER evaluation.

Severe head injury is unmistakable. The hallmarks include worsening headache, repeated vomiting, prolonged loss of consciousness, and seizures. Other red flags are blurred or double vision, slurred speech, weakness on one side, fluid from the nose or ears, and unequal pupils.

If any severe symptoms are present, call 911 immediately. The next section covers the specific red flags that turn a head injury into an emergency.

Red Flag Symptoms: When a Head Injury Becomes an Emergency

The red flag symptoms for a head injury all share one thing: they signal pressure inside the skull, bleeding, or nerve damage. Each one alone is a 911 call.

  • Vomiting more than once: single vomit is common with concussion, but repeated vomiting points to rising intracranial pressure.
  • Worsening or severe headache: pain that climbs from a 4 to a 9 over an hour suggests an evolving bleed or swelling.
  • Confusion, slurred speech, or trouble waking up: signs the brain is not functioning normally.
  • Unequal pupil sizes: known as anisocoria, often a late sign of brain herniation pressure.
  • Seizure: even a brief one after a head injury is a 911 call.
  • Clear or blood-tinged fluid from the nose or ears: cerebrospinal fluid leaking through a basilar skull fracture.
  • Weakness, numbness, or paralysis on one side: points to brain or spinal cord injury.
  • Repeated falls or coordination loss: suggests the cerebellum or brainstem has been affected.

None of these is a "watch and see" symptom. The brain has limited room to swell inside the skull, and once pressure rises, every minute of delay matters.

Head Injuries in Children: Why Thresholds Differ

Children are not small adults when it comes to head injuries. Their thinner skulls, larger heads relative to body size, and developing brains create a different risk profile.

The biggest practical difference: children have a lower threshold for ER evaluation. A toddler who falls from a changing table or a child who falls off a bike at moderate speed often needs imaging. Even if they look fine, the threshold is lower.

Per the CDC HEADS UP program, parents should bring a child to the ER for any of these:

  • Loss of consciousness, even briefly
  • Vomiting (any episode in a child under 2; more than one in older children)
  • Persistent crying or inconsolability in infants and toddlers
  • Severe or worsening headache in children old enough to describe it
  • Seizure
  • Bulging soft spot in infants
  • Visible scalp deformity or large swelling

For the broader pediatric decision rule, see our child hit head guide. For concussion-specific care, see our concussion treatment page.

When to Call 911 vs Same-Day Doctor for Head Injuries

Call 911 immediately if any of these are present:

  • Loss of consciousness, however brief
  • Seizure after the injury
  • Repeated vomiting
  • Severe or worsening headache
  • Confusion that does not clear within 5 minutes
  • Slurred speech, blurred or double vision, weakness on one side
  • Clear fluid or blood from the nose or ears
  • Unequal pupils
  • Cannot be roused from sleep
  • Any head injury in someone on a blood thinner

Do not drive yourself or the patient. Paramedics can stabilize the airway, control bleeding, and notify the hospital so imaging is ready on arrival.

See your primary care doctor or visit urgent care within 24 hours if the symptoms are mild but persistent. The pattern fits if you have a steady headache that has not eased, brief confusion that resolved, or a small scalp wound that is not bleeding heavily.

Schedule a regular doctor visit if the bump or bruise has no other symptoms after 24 hours of monitoring. If you cannot decide which path is right, our medical emergency signs guide walks through the broader 911-versus-PCP rule. Our ER vs urgent care guide covers what each setting handles best.

Preventing Head Injuries

Most head injuries are preventable. The standard prevention measures cover four big categories.

Helmets reduce serious head injury by 60% or more in cycling, motorcycling, contact sports, skiing, and skating. Wear them every ride.

Seatbelts and child car seats prevent the deceleration injuries that cause most TBIs in motor vehicle crashes. After a crash, even a minor one, see our car accident guide for what to watch for.

Fall prevention in older adults includes removing rugs that slide, installing grab bars in bathrooms, treating low blood pressure, and addressing vision problems early. Falls are the leading cause of head injury in adults over 65.

Workplace safety includes hard hats on construction sites, fall protection at heights, and immediate reporting of any head impact.

Recovery and Follow-Up Care

Recovery from a head injury follows three stages, each with its own rules.

Acute phase (0 to 72 hours): rest, hydration, and someone available to monitor for the red flag symptoms in the previous section. No driving, no alcohol, no strenuous exercise. Avoid screens and bright light if symptoms get worse with stimulation.

Subacute phase (1 to 2 weeks): gradual cognitive return. School-age children often need shortened school days and screen-time limits for a week or two. Adults with concussion typically return to desk work in 7 to 10 days, with cognitive rest breaks built in.

Return-to-activity phase: graded progression back to full activity, with each step lasting at least 24 hours. Per Mayo Clinic, returning to contact sports too early raises the risk of second-impact syndrome, which can be fatal in adolescents.

If symptoms persist beyond 4 weeks for adults or 6 weeks for children, the diagnosis becomes post-concussion syndrome. This warrants a referral to a neurologist or sports-medicine specialist.

FAQs

How long should I watch someone after a head bump?

Monitor for 24 to 48 hours after any head injury that caused a noticeable bump, brief dizziness, or a short headache. The first 24 hours is when delayed bleeding most often shows up.

Wake the person every 2 to 3 hours during the first night to confirm they can be roused and answer simple questions. If they cannot be roused, call 911.

When does a bump become an ER trip?

The bump alone is rarely the issue. The ER trip is triggered by associated symptoms: any loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, severe or worsening headache, confusion, seizure, or unequal pupils.

Without those symptoms, a small scalp bump can be watched at home with the 24-hour monitoring routine. With any of those symptoms, the trip happens immediately.

Concussion vs traumatic brain injury: what is the difference?

A concussion is a mild type of traumatic brain injury (TBI). All concussions are TBIs, but TBI as a category also includes moderate and severe injuries that concussion does not cover. These include contusion, hematoma, and diffuse axonal injury.

The clinical distinction matters for prognosis. Most concussions resolve fully in 7 to 14 days. Moderate or severe TBIs can take months and sometimes leave permanent deficits.

Is a child's head injury more dangerous than an adult's?

Not always more dangerous, but the threshold for ER evaluation is lower for children. Their thinner skulls, larger heads relative to body size, and developing brains change the risk profile.

A child also cannot always describe symptoms accurately. Persistent crying, refusing to eat, unusual sleepiness, or a bulging soft spot in infants are signs that warrant ER evaluation even without obvious external injury.

How long does head injury recovery take?

Mild concussion: 7 to 14 days for most adults, sometimes up to 4 weeks. Children often take a bit longer, sometimes 6 weeks.

Moderate to severe TBI: weeks to months, with rehabilitation needed for cognitive recovery. Some deficits may persist long-term and need ongoing therapy.

Should I wake someone up after a head injury?

For 24 hours after a moderate head injury, yes. Wake the person every 2 to 3 hours overnight. Confirm they can be roused and answer simple questions about who they are and where they are.

If they cannot be roused, or if their answers are confused, call 911. Inability to wake from sleep after a head injury is a red flag for rising intracranial pressure.

Suppose you are given no clues to a mystery; how would you solve it? That is how the diagnosis of disease would occur without medical imaging. Diagnostic imaging offers doctors the ability to see inside the body with minimal risk, to a clear picture, and in most cases in real time, without performing surgery. Such tests have revolutionized the manner in which we identify, treat, and even prevent illness. Millions of imaging processes occur every year in the U.S., be it the routine X-rays or the high-end MRIs and PET scans. According to the CDC, these operations are the necessary instruments in contemporary healthcare. For patients, that means faster answers, fewer invasive procedures, and more confidence in their care.

What Is Diagnostic Imaging?

What is the meaning of diagnostic imaging?

Diagnostic imaging is a medical procedure that produces images of the inner body by energy sources such as X-rays, sound waves, magnetic fields, or radioactive materials. MedlinePlus states that these images help doctors evaluate bones, tissues, and organs without surgery

Is diagnostic imaging the same as an MRI?

Not exactly. MRI is one of the diagnostic imaging techniques that has numerous other types, which include CT scans, ultrasounds, and X-rays.

What is an example of a diagnostic imaging test?

Examples include chest X-rays, pregnancy ultrasounds, brain MRIs, or PET scans for cancer detection.

Why do I need diagnostic imaging?

Doctors may order imaging to:
  • Confirm or rule out a diagnosis
  • Detect disease early
  • Plan surgery or other treatment
  • Monitor progress over time
According to the CDC, millions of these tests are done annually because it is important to do non-invasive diagnosis correctly.

What Are the Main Types of Diagnostic Imaging?

How many types of diagnostic imaging are there?

The most popular ones are nuclear medicine, MRI, CT, X-ray, and ultrasound, while there are more. 

What is major diagnostic imaging?

The “big four” in most hospitals are:
  1. X-rays – best for bones and chest.
  2. CT scans – fast, detailed cross-sections.
  3. MRI – detailed pictures of soft tissue, brain, and spine.
  4. Ultrasound – safe, radiation-free, commonly used in pregnancy.

Which is more diagnostic, CT or MRI?

Both have strengths:
  • CT scans are faster and excellent for trauma, chest, and abdomen.
  • MRIs are better for soft tissues like the brain, spinal cord, and joints.

Which three diagnostic tests use a camera to visualize internal structures?

Endoscopy, colonoscopy, and capsule endoscopy involve tiny cameras, but they’re considered imaging in a broader sense, not radiology.

Which of the following is a common type of diagnostic imaging?

According to the CDC, the most common is the X-ray, followed closely by CT scans.

Is Diagnostic Imaging the Same as a CT Scan?

Are CT scans considered diagnostic imaging?

Indeed, one of the most used types of diagnostic imaging is a CT scan. They produce 3D cross-sectional pictures using X-rays. 

What is a CT scan for the knee?

In order to identify fractures or arthritis, a CT scan of the knee offers detailed pictures of the bones, ligaments, and surrounding tissues.

What is diagnostic imaging also called?

It’s also known as medical imaging or radiology imaging.

What does diagnostic imaging cover?

PAHO states that it covers a wide range of tests, including:
  • Bone and joint injuries
  • Heart and lung conditions
  • Brain and spinal cord disorders
  • Cancer detection and monitoring
  • Organ function through nuclear medicine.

What Is the Highest Paying Medical Imaging Job?

Medical imaging isn’t just life-saving; it’s also a growing career field. Many patients wonder who interprets or performs these scans, and which roles earn the most.

Do ultrasound or MRI techs make more?

Typically, MRI technologists earn more on average, though salaries vary by location and specialization.

Who makes more, an RN or a radiology tech?

Registered Nurses (RNs) and radiology technologists both play vital roles. On average, RNs often earn more, but advanced imaging technologists can exceed RN salaries.

Who gets paid more, a radiation therapist or a sonographer?

Radiation therapists generally have higher earning potential compared to sonographers, reflecting the advanced training required.

Which medical technologist makes the most money?

Specialized radiology roles, such as MRI, CT, and nuclear medicine technologists, are often among the highest paid in diagnostic imaging.

Do CT or MRI techs make more money?

MRI techs tend to earn slightly higher salaries due to the complexity of MRI scans.

What imaging career pays the most?

According to the NIH, Radiation therapists, MRI technologists, and nuclear medicine technologists are usually the top earners in the imaging field.

Risks and Safety in Diagnostic Imaging

While diagnostic imaging is safe for most people, some procedures involve radiation. The CDC stresses that radiation doses are kept as low as possible.
  • X-ray & CT scans: Use ionizing radiation but at controlled doses.
  • MRI & Ultrasound: No radiation, safe for most patients, including pregnant women.
  • Contrast agents: Sometimes used; rarely cause allergic reactions.
Doctors always weigh benefits vs. risks, ensuring imaging is only done when medically needed.

Take the Next Step With ER of Lufkin

Diagnostic imaging is one of the most powerful tools in modern medicine. If your doctor recommends an imaging test, don’t delay. These procedures can save lives by detecting problems early and guiding treatment.  At the ER of Lufkin, your health and peace of mind are our top priorities. Whether you need diagnostic imaging, emergency care, or other advanced medical services, our team is here 24/7 to provide fast, accurate answers and compassionate treatment. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs

What are the three main types of diagnostic imaging?

X-ray, CT, and MRI are considered the three primary types.

Is diagnostic imaging the same as an MRI?

No, MRI is one type of diagnostic imaging.

Are CT scans diagnostic imaging?

Yes, CT is one of the most widely used forms.

Which imaging test is safest?

Ultrasound and MRI, since they don’t use radiation.

What imaging career pays the most?

Radiation therapists and MRI technologists typically top the list.

Do imaging tests hurt?

Most are painless; some may cause brief discomfort.

How long does it take to get results?

X-rays may be available within hours, MRIs and CTs may take 1–2 days.

Does ER of Lufkin offer diagnostic imaging?

Yes. At the ER of Lufkin, we provide advanced diagnostic imaging, including X-rays, CT scans, and ultrasound. Our on-site imaging helps patients get fast answers and the right treatment without delay.

  • Cancer detection and monitoring
  • Organ function through nuclear medicine.

What Is the Highest Paying Medical Imaging Job?

Medical imaging isn’t just life-saving; it’s also a growing career field. Many patients wonder who interprets or performs these scans, and which roles earn the most.

Do ultrasound or MRI techs make more?

Typically, MRI technologists earn more on average, though salaries vary by location and specialization.

Who makes more, an RN or a radiology tech?

Registered Nurses (RNs) and radiology technologists both play vital roles. On average, RNs often earn more, but advanced imaging technologists can exceed RN salaries.

Who gets paid more, a radiation therapist or a sonographer?

Radiation therapists generally have higher earning potential compared to sonographers, reflecting the advanced training required.

Which medical technologist makes the most money?

Specialized radiology roles, such as MRI, CT, and nuclear medicine technologists, are often among the highest paid in diagnostic imaging.

Do CT or MRI techs make more money?

MRI techs tend to earn slightly higher salaries due to the complexity of MRI scans.

What imaging career pays the most?

According to the NIH, Radiation therapists, MRI technologists, and nuclear medicine technologists are usually the top earners in the imaging field.

Risks and Safety in Diagnostic Imaging

While diagnostic imaging is safe for most people, some procedures involve radiation. The CDC stresses that radiation doses are kept as low as possible.

  • X-ray & CT scans: Use ionizing radiation but at controlled doses.
  • MRI & Ultrasound: No radiation, safe for most patients, including pregnant women.
  • Contrast agents: Sometimes used; rarely cause allergic reactions.

Doctors always weigh benefits vs. risks, ensuring imaging is only done when medically needed.

One of the most widespread health problems that is experienced by millions of people annually is a sore throat. It might sound like a minor inconvenience, though in fact, it may be indicative of a more severe underlying disorder.

Knowing what sore throats are and how they are treated, and preventing further complications is possible by learning all about their causes, symptoms, and effective treatment.

Within this blog post, we will explore the various causes of sore throats, natural remedies, over-the-counter medication, and when to seek medical attention.

At the end, you will be more aware of what stretches to alleviate your sore throat and when it is time to seek medical help.

What is a Sore Throat?

Understanding the Basics of a Sore Throat

Sore throat takes the form of pain, scratchiness, or irritation in the throat that, in most cases, makes swallowing or talking painful. It might be from a light irritation to intense pain. T

he infection is one of the causes of sore throats, and it may also be caused by other factors, such as allergies, irritants, or overly dry air. Actually, one of the most frequent symptoms of most upper respiratory diseases, such as a cold, flu, or strep throat, is a sore throat.

According to the CDC, sore throats have become a prevalent health issue that may develop in any person of any age. The good news is that the majority of sore throats heal themselves over time and with adequate care, yet understanding the cause would be significant in choosing the most appropriate treatment strategy.

What Causes a Sore Throat?

Common Causes of a Sore Throat

  1. Viral Infections: Viral infections (such as common cold, influenza, COVID-19) are the cause of a majority of throat soreness. These are mild types of infections, which in most cases clear within a week.
  2. Bacterial Infections: Strep throat is also a kind of infection that may result in severe throat pain. Bacterial infections have to be treated with antibiotics, unlike viral infections.
  3. Allergies and Irritants: Throat inflammation can result as a result of allergies to pollen or dust, pet dander, or mold. Moreover, colds such as smoke, pollution, or chemicals may worsen throat pain.
  4. Dry Air and Dehydration: Breathing dry air, particularly in the winter season, can result in a sore throat. Dry throat may also attest to dehydration.

Rare Causes of a Sore Throat

  • In others, a sore throat can be due to even more serious problems, such as autoimmune disorders, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), or cancer. However, these causes are far less common.

How Long Does a Sore Throat Last?

Typical Duration of a Sore Throat

A sore throat’s duration depends largely on its cause:

  • Viral sore throats: They are generally between 3 to 7 days. The immunity manages to overcome the virus, and the symptoms would improve in most cases.
  • Bacterial sore throats: Bacteriogenic sore throats may take a longer time before mild symptoms may result unless natural antibiotics are prescribed.
  • Chronic sore throat: When the sore throat continues after one week or occurs several times, then it might be an indicator of a more severe problem, which could include GERD or an infection that should be treated with medicine.

Stages of a Sore Throat

The stage of the virus might affect how severe a sore throat is:

  • Early Stage: Mild irritation or scratchiness in the throat.
  • Middle Stage: Throat pain becomes more noticeable, especially when swallowing.
  • Severe Stage: Swollen lymph nodes, fever, and difficulty swallowing may occur.

How to Relieve a Sore Throat

Natural Remedies for Sore Throat Relief

  1. Gargling Salt Water: Another method of treating a sore throat is by heating and pouring salt water, which in turn can clean and get rid of the mucus as well as reduce inflammation. Add one teaspoon of salt to a glass of warm water and gargle a few times throughout the day.
  2. Drinking Warm Liquids: If consumed in the form of teas, teas that contain honey and lemon may help in soothing. Honey is an anti-inflammatory, and lemon loosens mucus.
  3. Using a Humidifier: Adding moisture to the air can help alleviate the dryness that worsens throat irritation, especially during colder months.
  4. Resting Your Voice and Staying Hydrated:  You should not push your voice too hard, and you must be consuming enough fluids to make sure that your throat stays hydrated.

For more natural remedies, check the Osteopathic Health 

Over-the-Counter Medications for Sore Throat

  • Pain Relievers: Over-the-counter medications like acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) can reduce pain and inflammation.
  • Lozenges and Sprays: Medicated lozenges and throat sprays can help numb the throat and alleviate discomfort temporarily.
  • Antihistamines: If allergies are the cause, antihistamines like Claritin or Benadryl can help alleviate symptoms.

What is the Fastest Way to Cure a Sore Throat?

When to Use Medication vs. Home Remedies

With less serious viral infections, treatment with home measures such as saltwater gargles or warm tea is usually adequate. But, when your sore throat is bacterial (strep throat), you can use antibiotics to wipe out the infection.

How to Reduce Throat Pain Naturally

  • Steam Inhalation: Inhaling steam from a bowl of hot water can help loosen mucus and relieve throat irritation.
  • Honey and Lemon: These can soothe and lubricate the throat, reducing pain and inflammation.

When Should You Seek Medical Attention for a Sore Throat?

Signs You Should See a Doctor

  • High fever (above 101°F)
  • Severe difficulty swallowing or breathing
  • Persistent symptoms lasting more than a week
  • Swollen lymph nodes or a rash
  • You suspect you may have strep throat

As the CDC states, consult your healthcare provider if you experience any of the above symptoms. For more information.

What to Expect During a Medical Visit

  • Your doctor may perform a throat swab test to check for strep throat.
  • If it’s a viral infection, your doctor will likely recommend rest and symptom management. If it's bacterial, antibiotics will be prescribed.

Need Relief from a Sore Throat?

If you're struggling with a sore throat that’s making it hard to swallow, speak, or even breathe comfortably, it's time to take action. Whether it's from a viral infection, allergies, or something more serious, we’re here to help.

Visit us today at the ER of Lufkin or call for immediate assistance. We’re here 24/7 to ensure your health is in good hands.

Need Immediate Care? Call Us Now at (936) 427-1313

Stay informed with seasonal health tips, first aid advice, and practical ways to maintain your well-being throughout the year. Follow ER of Lufkin on Facebook and Instagram for valuable health updates.

FAQs 

What is the best medicine for a sore throat?

Pain relievers like acetaminophen or ibuprofen, along with throat lozenges, can help alleviate symptoms. Antibiotics may be necessary for bacterial infections like strep throat.

Can I take medicine for a sore throat while pregnant?

Always consult with your healthcare provider before taking any medication during pregnancy, including pain relievers.

What causes a sore throat in children?

Children often get sore throats from viral infections like the common cold, strep throat, or allergies.

Why does my throat hurt, but I’m not sick?

Throat pain can occur due to environmental factors such as dry air, allergies, or irritants like smoke, even if you're not "sick."

How long should a sore throat last?

Most viral sore throats last 3-7 days. If it persists or worsens, it may be time to consult a healthcare provider.

 Does ER of Lufkin provide treatment for sore throats?

Yes, the ER of Lufkin provides treatment for severe sore throats. If you're experiencing a sore throat with symptoms like high fever or difficulty swallowing, they offer emergency care services. 

Is Lufkin's ER open 24 hours a day?

Yes! The ER of Lufkin is open 24/7 to provide immediate care for medical emergencies, including heart attacks, injuries, respiratory issues, and more.

Do I need an appointment to visit the ER of Lufkin?

No, you do not need an appointment to visit the ER of Lufkin. We are open 24/7 to provide immediate care for all medical emergencies. Just walk in, and our team will be ready to assist you.

Is the ER of Lufkin covered by my insurance?

ER of Lufkin accepts a variety of insurance plans. It’s always a good idea to confirm coverage with your provider ahead of time, but we also provide billing options for self-pay patients. Please call our office or check with your insurance company for more details.
